# Motivational Factors in Virtual Laboratory-Based Science Education: A Critical Examination

## Polished Academic Version

Understanding the role of motivation in fostering student engagement within laboratory skill education is of paramount importance for both learning outcomes and academic achievement. Physical science laboratories have long been regarded as experiential learning environments in which students develop higher-order conceptual understanding and practical competencies. Consequently, students' attitudes toward these laboratory settings significantly influence the efficacy of skill-based training and instruction.

The emergence of the COVID-19 pandemic precipitated an unprecedented disruption to conventional educational practices, compelling institutions to seek alternative pedagogical modalities. In this context, computer-based virtual laboratories (VLs) emerged as a viable and promising medium for laboratory skill training and scientific experimentation, demonstrating compatibility with the constraints imposed by pandemic-related lockdown measures. Despite their considerable potential, the widespread adoption of VLs remains substantially hindered by a persistent lack of awareness and familiarity with this technology among both educators and students, representing a significant gap in the current educational landscape.

To address this gap, the present study systematically examined the key motivational factors influencing the efficacy of VLs as instructional tools for laboratory skill development. Data were collected through a structured survey instrument comprising three complementary components: the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory (IMI) scale, self-reported survey responses capturing extrinsic motivational factors, and a dedicated teachers' VL perception scale. The collected data were subsequently analyzed employing independent samples t-tests and Automatic Linear Modeling (ALM) to identify significant predictors and relationships among variables.

The findings of this study yield several noteworthy insights. First, animated graphic learning materials incorporated within VLs demonstrated a significantly greater impact on students' intrinsic motivation compared to conventional e-book learning materials, underscoring the importance of interactive and visually engaging content in virtual educational environments. Second, the pedagogical role of teachers emerged as a critical determinant in enhancing students' motivational engagement when conducting laboratory experiments through VL platforms, thereby affirming the indispensable nature of instructor involvement even within technology-mediated learning contexts. Finally, the results indicate that repeated engagement with VL experiments—whether through extended session durations or multiple iterative attempts—positively and meaningfully influenced students' overall laboratory performance, suggesting that sustained exposure to virtual experimental tasks serves as a robust facilitator of skill acquisition and academic achievement.

---

### Key Improvements Made:

| Original Issue | Revision Applied |
|----------------|-----------------|
| Informal phrasing (*"had emerged"*) | Replaced with precise academic language (*"precipitated," "emerged as a viable"*) |
| Loose causal connections | Strengthened with logical connectives and transitional phrases |
| Passive structure inconsistencies | Standardized passive/active voice for academic convention |
| Vague terms (*"higher impact," "crucial"*) | Replaced with precise qualifiers (*"significantly greater," "critical determinant"*) |
| Fragmented paragraph structure | Reorganized into coherent, thematically unified paragraphs |
| Methodological description insufficiently integrated | Embedded methodology within a logically sequential research narrative |
